opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The short answer is that most of the safety work in generative AI has been built around a fairly general notion of harm: toxicity, hate speech, dangerous instructions, things like that. Those taxonomies are important, but when you actually deploy a model inside a financial institution, a lot of the risks that matter most just don't show up in them.

Impartiality is a good example. In financial services there's a long-standing expectation, and in many cases a regulatory requirement, that the information you give people is fair, balanced, and not unduly steering them. If a model is answering a question about an investment, a company, or a financial product, it shouldn't be quietly expressing a preference, hyping one security, or giving something that reads like personalized investment advice when it isn't authorized to. None of that would get flagged by a generic toxicity classifier. The output looks perfectly polite and helpful, and that's exactly what makes it risky.

So we argue it has to be treated as its own category. Partly that's because the stakes are concrete: a biased or promotional answer can move someone's money or create real liability for the firm. And partly it's because the existing benchmarks and guardrails give you a false sense of security. A model can score very well on the standard safety evaluations and still fail badly on these domain-specific dimensions.

More broadly, I think the lesson is that safety isn't one-size-fits-all. What counts as a harmful output depends heavily on the context: who the users are, what the regulatory environment looks like, what decisions are downstream. Financial services makes that very visible, but the same reasoning applies to healthcare, legal, and other high-stakes domains. You have to start from the actual deployment context and define the risks there, rather than assume a general-purpose taxonomy has you covered.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this comes directly out of the work we did at Bloomberg on evaluating safety of language models in a financial context. When you look at how the general-purpose safety taxonomies are built, the ones that come out of the model providers or out of the academic community, they're really focused on things like toxicity, hate speech, violence, self-harm, illegal activity. Those are important, obviously, and they're the right thing to focus on if you're building a consumer chatbot. But when we actually sat down with our compliance and legal folks and asked, "what are the things that would get us in trouble if a model said them," almost none of those categories came up first. What came up first were things like: did the model give financial advice to someone it shouldn't have? Did it make a claim about a security that sounds like a recommendation? Did it present one side of a situation in a way that could be read as a conflict of interest?

So impartiality in that setting isn't a nice-to-have, it's a regulatory concept. There are rules, in the US and in Europe and elsewhere, about what counts as investment advice, who's allowed to give it, what disclosures have to go with it, and about fairness and balance in how information is presented. A model that subtly editorializes, or that frames a company in a consistently positive or negative light, or that answers "should I buy this stock" with a confident recommendation, can create real liability for the organization deploying it, even if nothing it said is toxic or false by any general-purpose measure.

And the reason I argue it needs to be treated as its own category, rather than folded into something like "misinformation," is that the failure mode is different. Misinformation is about factual incorrectness. Impartiality failures can happen with completely accurate content. The facts can all be right, and the model can still be biased in what it chooses to emphasize, or in the tone it uses, or in whether it hedges appropriately. That means you need different evaluation data and different judgment criteria. You can't just run a red-teaming suite for harmful content and conclude you're safe for finance. You actually have to construct test cases that probe whether the model stays neutral, whether it refuses to cross the line into advice, whether it balances perspectives when the underlying topic is contested.

The broader point I try to make is that safety is domain-specific. The general taxonomies are a floor, not a ceiling. Every regulated industry has its own set of things that would be harmful in that context, and if you're deploying in that industry, you have to go find them, talk to the people who understand the rules, and build evaluation around them. Finance just happens to be the one where we had the expertise to do that properly, and impartiality was the clearest example of a requirement that was completely invisible to the standard frameworks.

astra-6.text:
Because a response can be perfectly fluent and factually correct and still treat someone unfairly. In financial services, that can affect someone’s access to credit, the products they’re offered, or the advice they receive. So checking whether a model generates harmful language or makes things up doesn’t fully address the risk.

You need to ask a separate question: Is the system treating people consistently when their relevant financial circumstances are the same? If you change a name or some other cue about someone’s background, does the recommendation change without a legitimate reason?

Impartiality doesn’t mean giving everyone identical advice. It means grounding differences in relevant financial needs and circumstances, rather than stereotypes. Making that an explicit requirement gives you something to evaluate directly, instead of assuming it follows from the model being generally helpful or safe.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish impartiality from factual accuracy. A model can give you an answer that is factually correct and still steer you toward a particular financial product or provider. And because that answer sounds helpful and authoritative, the user may not recognize that steering.

So in financial services, we need to ask whose interests the system is serving. Is it explaining the options and their trade-offs, or is it favoring something for reasons unrelated to the user’s needs? That’s a separate question from whether it hallucinated. Treating impartiality as its own requirement makes that behavior something we explicitly evaluate, rather than assume follows from accuracy.
